lesson.title: Cloud service models and shared responsibility
lesson.why: Managed services remove some operational work, not accountability for the application. A public database caused by an access mistake remains a customer problem even when the provider patches every underlying server.
lesson.what: Service models divide control between customer and provider. Select a model by identifying who operates each layer, then verify the actual service contract rather than assuming that all managed offerings have identical boundaries.

concepts.name: Infrastructure control
concepts.body: With infrastructure as a service, the provider operates facilities and virtualization while the customer typically configures the guest operating system, applications, identities and data. Guest patching remains work. A machine image is a starting point, not a lifetime patch guarantee.

concepts.name: Platform boundaries
concepts.body: A managed platform commonly operates the runtime or database engine. Customers still choose supported versions, configure access and protect data. Backup features need retention and restore decisions; the existence of a backup button does not prove recovery meets business requirements.

concepts.name: Software consumption
concepts.body: Software as a service transfers more application operation to the vendor. Tenant administrators still control users, sharing, retention and integrations. An approved employee sharing a confidential document publicly is not prevented merely by choosing a software subscription.

concepts.name: Shared controls
concepts.body: Responsibility can be shared within one control: providers encrypt physical media while customers manage authorization and sometimes keys. Write separate accountable owners for configuration, evidence and incident response. A gap between owners is more dangerous than a clearly assigned manual task.

e2e: List the application data and recovery needs before comparing service models.
Map facilities, host, guest, runtime, application and identity to explicit owners.
Check service documentation for exceptions such as customer-managed engine upgrades.
Test access and restoration in a paper scenario, then assign unresolved actions.

tasks.name: Map six layers
steps: Offline, make six rows: facility, hypervisor, guest OS, application, identity and data. For a typical VM mark the first two provider-operated and the remaining four customer-operated. Explain why customer data classification cannot be delegated to the hypervisor.

tasks.name: Compare database options
steps: Compare a database on a VM with a managed database. Move host patching and routine engine operation toward the provider only where documented. Keep schema design, database users and retention decisions with the customer; record a restore-test owner.

tasks.name: Calculate ownership coverage
steps: A fictional service has 12 required controls: seven provider-owned, four customer-owned and one unassigned. Coverage is 11/12 = 91.7 percent, not complete. Assign certificate renewal to an owner and specify an expiry alert as evidence.

tasks.name: Rehearse tenant exposure
steps: A hypothetical SaaS folder is shared publicly. Write the sequence: restrict sharing, preserve access evidence, identify exposed data and notify the incident owner. Do not upload real files or change an actual tenant to demonstrate the mistake.

key_terms: IaaS: rented infrastructure with customer guest control.
PaaS: managed application or data platform.
SaaS: vendor-operated application.
Control owner: accountable party for an outcome.
lesson.safety: Use fictional identities and paper mappings only. Do not provision services or test public access with personal data.
cleanup: Discard fictional sharing links and retain only the responsibility matrix; no cloud resources were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical team says its managed database means security and backups need no customer work. How would you correct the plan?
interview_points: Separate provider infrastructure duties from customer access and data duties.
Check the specific service's version and backup boundaries.
Assign retention, restore testing and incident ownership.
Use evidence of recovery, not the service label, to judge readiness.

foundations/cloud-service-models-and-sha.core: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS shift operating boundaries, not all accountability. Map controls to owners per service. Identity, data classification, configuration and recovery verification remain explicit customer decisions.
objectives: Map infrastructure and application controls to owners.
Identify gaps in a managed-service responsibility matrix.
prerequisites: Understand applications, operating systems and stored data.

storyboard.title: Who closes the access gap?
storyboard.objective: Trace a customer access decision across a managed-service boundary.

scenes.title: Separate duties
scenes.caption: Engine maintenance and tenant authorization have different owners.
scenes.narration: The provider maintains the engine while the tenant administrator grants database access. Both controls are necessary.

scenes.title: Ownership gap
scenes.caption: Patching cannot repair an overly broad tenant grant.
scenes.narration: A broad customer grant exposes records even though the engine is current. Infrastructure maintenance did not authorize this sharing.

scenes.title: Restore the boundary
scenes.caption: The customer narrows access and records evidence.
scenes.narration: The administrator removes the broad grant, checks access evidence and assigns recurring reviews without transferring responsibility to the provider.

lesson.title: Regions availability zones and fault domains
lesson.why: Two servers are not necessarily two independent failure domains. Redundancy helps only when the surviving path retains capacity, connectivity and the data required to serve requests after a realistic shared failure.
lesson.what: A region is a geographic deployment area; availability zones divide regional infrastructure into isolated locations. Application failure domains also include shared configuration, identity, network paths and software releases, which may cross every physical zone.

concepts.name: Physical separation
concepts.body: Zones reduce correlated facility failures but do not eliminate regional dependencies. A region usually contains multiple zones connected with low latency. Service capabilities vary; explicitly confirm whether a selected service is zonal, regional or requires customer configuration for redundancy.

concepts.name: Logical correlation
concepts.body: A broken configuration pushed everywhere can defeat excellent physical separation. Shared DNS, credentials, deployment pipelines and databases create logical failure domains. Draw them alongside servers so the diagram does not imply independence where a common control still exists.

concepts.name: Data placement
concepts.body: Replicas need a defined replication mode and failover process. Synchronous replication can reduce acknowledged-write loss but adds coordination latency. Asynchronous replication permits lag, so a healthy second region may still lack the newest records when the first region disappears.

concepts.name: Survivor capacity
concepts.body: Redundant instances must carry the remaining traffic. Two equal zones normally serving half the demand each need enough spare capacity for the full load during a zone failure. Autoscaling may help, but quotas and provisioning time make immediate capacity an assumption to test.

e2e: Identify user traffic, authoritative data and shared dependencies in the request path.
Place replicas across intended physical domains and document remaining common controls.
Choose health detection and failover rules that prevent writes to competing primaries.
Calculate surviving capacity and rehearse recovery against the required data-loss window.

tasks.name: Draw failure boundaries
steps: Sketch two application replicas in different zones and one database in only the first zone. Trace a read after that zone disappears. The expected conclusion is database unavailability despite a surviving application replica, not automatic high availability.

tasks.name: Size the survivor
steps: Use fictional demand of 600 requests per second and two zones rated at 400 each. Normal load is 300 per zone; failure leaves a 200-request deficit. Three 300-capacity zones retain 600 after one fails, before safety margin.

tasks.name: Reason about lag
steps: An asynchronous replica is eight seconds behind while writes arrive at ten records per second. Estimate roughly 80 recent records at risk if the primary is lost. Explain why this estimate is not a guaranteed bound without measured lag.

tasks.name: Test a common failure
steps: On paper, deploy a malformed setting to both zones. Specify staged rollout, validation and a known-good configuration rollback. Contrast this recovery with a facility outage; adding another zone alone would copy the same software mistake.

key_terms: Region: geographic service deployment area.
Zone: isolated regional infrastructure location.
Fault domain: components sharing a failure cause.
Replication lag: delay before a replica receives changes.
lesson.safety: Use topology sketches and fictional traffic. Do not stop production instances, alter routing or launch paid replicas.
cleanup: Keep the capacity worksheet and remove any misleading labels claiming proven independence.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical two-zone service fails when one zone is lost even though its second application replica is healthy. What would you investigate?
interview_points: Trace the database and other shared dependencies.
Measure surviving capacity rather than counting replicas.
Check failover detection, routes and write authority.
Distinguish zone failures from shared configuration failures.

foundations/regions-availability-zones-a.core: Count independent failure paths, not servers. Check regional versus zonal service behavior, replication lag, write authority and capacity after failure. Physical separation does not protect against a globally deployed bad configuration.
objectives: Calculate capacity remaining after a zone loss.
prerequisites: Understand client-server requests and replicated data.

storyboard.title: A surviving zone needs data and capacity
storyboard.objective: Follow traffic when a zonal dependency fails.

scenes.title: Balanced traffic
scenes.caption: Both zones share demand and access durable data.
scenes.narration: Traffic uses both application zones. Database placement and spare capacity determine whether either zone can survive alone.

scenes.title: Zone A fails
scenes.caption: A healthy replica does not guarantee sufficient capacity.
scenes.narration: Zone A becomes unavailable. The router shifts demand, but Zone B must now serve twice its normal traffic.

scenes.title: Validate the surviving path
scenes.caption: Check capacity, database reachability and write authority.
scenes.narration: The operator verifies database access and survivor capacity before declaring recovery. A reachable application without data is not success.

lesson.title: Virtualization and hypervisors
lesson.why: Virtual machines share physical resources while presenting separate operating systems. Understanding that boundary explains noisy-neighbor symptoms, virtual CPU scheduling and why adding guest memory cannot repair a slow shared storage device.
lesson.what: A hypervisor mediates guest execution and resource access. Hardware assistance supports isolation and privileged instruction handling; virtual devices expose compute, memory, disk and networking abstractions without making the underlying host infinitely fast.

concepts.name: Guest and host boundaries
concepts.body: A guest has its own kernel and virtual hardware. A type-one hypervisor runs directly on hardware; a hosted hypervisor relies on a host operating system. Implementation details vary, but both must schedule guest work and preserve isolation between workloads.

concepts.name: CPU scheduling
concepts.body: A virtual CPU is scheduled execution capacity, not necessarily a permanently dedicated physical core. Oversubscription improves utilization when guests are idle. Under contention, runnable guests wait; guest CPU utilization alone may miss time not granted by the hypervisor.

concepts.name: Memory mapping
concepts.body: Guest virtual addresses map through guest physical addresses to host memory. Hardware-assisted translation helps enforce separation. Ballooning and host reclamation can affect performance where supported. Swapping introduces storage latency, so allocating more apparent memory does not create physical memory.

concepts.name: Virtual devices and images
concepts.body: Virtual disks are backed by files, volumes or network storage. Snapshots may depend on a chain of earlier data and are not automatically independent backups. Paravirtualized drivers reduce emulation overhead, while compatible images still need updates and supported device drivers.

e2e: The guest application issues an instruction or requests a virtual device operation.
The guest kernel handles the request and the virtualization boundary enforces permitted access.
The host scheduler and storage backend provide actual resources when available.
The result returns to the guest; measure host contention before changing guest settings.

tasks.name: Label the stack
steps: Draw application, guest kernel, virtual CPU, hypervisor and physical core. Mark where guest scheduling ends and host scheduling begins. Explain why two guests can report different operating systems while sharing the same physical processor and network adapter.

tasks.name: Compute oversubscription
steps: Four guests each have four vCPUs on an eight-core host: 16/8 gives a 2:1 vCPU-to-core ratio. If every vCPU demands a full core simultaneously, capacity is insufficient. This ratio alone does not predict latency for mostly idle guests.

tasks.name: Diagnose contention offline
tasks.goal: Distinguish a busy guest from a busy host.
steps: Compare fictional samples: guest CPU 35 percent, rising request latency and elevated steal time where reported. Suspect scheduling contention; request host evidence. Contrast guest CPU 100 percent with low steal, which more strongly suggests guest-side CPU saturation.

tasks.name: Evaluate a snapshot claim
steps: A snapshot references a base disk on the same failed storage array. Explain why it cannot restore missing base blocks. Specify an independent backup location, application consistency checks and a restore rehearsal without taking a real VM snapshot.

key_terms: Hypervisor: mediator of virtual machine resources.
Guest: operating system inside a VM.
vCPU: schedulable virtual processor.
Overcommit: promised resources exceeding physical capacity.
lesson.safety: Use calculations only; do not modify host virtualization settings, allocate large VMs or change production memory reservations.
cleanup: Retain the resource diagram; discard hypothetical identifiers and do not delete real snapshots or disks.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical VM becomes slow although its application uses little CPU. How would you separate guest and host causes?
interview_points: Inspect scheduling delay or steal indicators where available.
Check disk latency and host memory pressure.
Compare affected guests and timing for shared contention.
Avoid assuming each vCPU is an exclusive physical core.

foundations/virtualization-and-hyperviso.core: VMs have separate guest kernels but share host scheduling and device backends. vCPU counts are not performance guarantees. Diagnose contention at both layers and distinguish dependent snapshots from independent, tested backups.
objectives: Calculate and qualify a CPU overcommit ratio.
prerequisites: Know the roles of a kernel, processor and disk.

storyboard.title: A virtual CPU waits for a physical core
storyboard.objective: Explain guest latency caused by host scheduling contention.

scenes.title: Execution is scheduled
scenes.caption: Virtual work consumes physical CPU time.
scenes.narration: The guest submits runnable work. The hypervisor schedules a virtual processor onto an available physical core.

scenes.title: Contending guests wait
scenes.caption: Idle-looking guest metrics can hide scheduling delay.
scenes.narration: Other guests occupy the cores. Runnable work waits at the hypervisor boundary, increasing latency without useful guest execution.

scenes.title: Diagnose before resizing
scenes.caption: Correlate guest delay with host contention evidence.
scenes.narration: The operator checks scheduling delay and host demand, then adjusts placement or capacity rather than blindly adding virtual processors.

lesson.title: Compute storage and network trade-offs
lesson.why: An application is limited by its slowest necessary resource, not by the largest number on a machine specification. Balancing CPU, storage access and network transfer prevents expensive upgrades that leave the actual bottleneck unchanged.
lesson.what: Resource selection begins with an access pattern and measurable objective. Compute performs work, storage persists or retrieves bytes, and networking moves them; serialization, queueing and data locality connect their performance characteristics.

concepts.name: Compute demand
concepts.body: CPU-bound work benefits from more execution capacity only when it can run concurrently. A single serial stage may limit total throughput. Memory capacity and bandwidth also matter: repeated allocation, garbage collection or cache misses can make a nominally fast processor ineffective.

concepts.name: Storage shape
concepts.body: Block storage presents addressable blocks, file storage offers filesystem semantics and object storage retrieves named objects through APIs. Compare access size, concurrency, durability and update semantics. A large sequential scan and many small random reads stress different storage limits.

concepts.name: Latency versus throughput
concepts.body: Bandwidth measures bytes per second; latency measures completion time. High bandwidth cannot eliminate a required remote round trip. IOPS multiplied by average operation size estimates throughput only when the device, queue depth and access pattern can sustain those operations.

concepts.name: Data locality
concepts.body: Moving computation toward its data can reduce transfers and latency. Caching may help repeated reads but introduces freshness and capacity decisions. Replication improves some read paths while adding write coordination and storage overhead; measure the full path rather than one component.

e2e: Characterize request rate, data size, read/write mix and required latency.
Estimate CPU time, storage operations and transferred bytes for each request.
Measure queues and percentiles at the constrained component using a stable workload.
Change one resource or access pattern and compare the same workload again.

tasks.name: Classify three workloads
steps: Offline, assign a VM boot disk to block storage, shared directory access to file storage and immutable report downloads to object storage. Document one exception for each: application semantics and provider capabilities outrank a simplistic product-category rule.

tasks.name: Calculate transfer time
steps: A 100 MB decimal payload crossing a 100 Mb/s link contains 800 megabits. Ideal transfer time is 800/100 = eight seconds, before protocol overhead or contention. Doubling CPU speed cannot make this link transfer the same bytes in four seconds.

tasks.name: Estimate storage demand
steps: At 2,000 operations per second with 4 KiB per operation, requested throughput is 8,000 KiB/s, about 7.81 MiB/s. Explain why a device advertising large sequential throughput may still miss a random-read latency target at this workload.

tasks.name: Choose the next experiment
steps: A hypothetical service has idle CPU, rising disk queues and unchanged response sizes. Propose reducing unnecessary reads or testing appropriate storage performance first. Hold request rate constant, compare tail latency and reject a change that only improves an unrelated metric.

key_terms: IOPS: completed input/output operations per second.
Bandwidth: achievable transfer rate.
Latency: elapsed operation time.
Locality: proximity of computation to required data.
lesson.safety: Perform offline estimates; do not benchmark shared disks, saturate networks or provision paid storage.
cleanup: Keep units and assumptions on the worksheet; remove unsupported claims of guaranteed vendor performance.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical report download remains slow after doubling application CPU. How would you find a better next change?
interview_points: Calculate the network transfer lower bound.
Inspect storage latency and queueing.
Separate serial work from parallelizable computation.
Compare identical workloads and include end-to-end latency.

foundations/compute-storage-and-network-.core: Choose resources from workload semantics and measurements. Distinguish bits from bytes, IOPS from throughput and latency from bandwidth. An upgrade helps only if it relieves the constrained part of the complete request path.
objectives: Calculate network and storage demand with consistent units.
prerequisites: Understand bytes, seconds and basic arithmetic.

storyboard.title: The network, not the CPU, limits delivery
storyboard.objective: Trace a report from computation through storage and transfer.

scenes.title: Generate and deliver
scenes.caption: The request includes both computation and data movement.
scenes.narration: The generator writes a report. Delivery then depends on storage reads and the client's available network throughput.

scenes.title: An ineffective upgrade
scenes.caption: A faster generator cannot bypass a saturated link.
scenes.narration: CPU capacity increases, but the hundred-megabit link still needs at least eight seconds for one hundred decimal megabytes.

scenes.title: Measure the constrained path
scenes.caption: Reduce bytes or improve transfer capacity after measurement.
scenes.narration: The operator measures transfer time and tests compression or a better delivery path, comparing the same report and client conditions.

lesson.title: Distributed systems fundamentals
lesson.why: A remote timeout is ambiguous: the other machine may have done the work and lost only the response. Treating every timeout as failure can duplicate payments, while waiting forever consumes capacity and blocks unrelated requests.
lesson.what: Distributed systems coordinate independent processes through messages with variable delay and partial failure. Their designs must specify what clients observe during retries, replication lag and partitions rather than assuming a single-machine sequence of events.

concepts.name: Partial failure
concepts.body: One process can fail while its peers continue. A missing response cannot reliably distinguish a slow server, a broken network and completed work whose acknowledgement was lost. Timeouts bound waiting; they provide suspicion, not proof that an operation never happened.

concepts.name: Idempotent effects
concepts.body: An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated. For create operations, a stable request identifier can connect retries to a stored result. Deduplication must share a durable boundary with the business effect or a crash can still allow duplicates.

concepts.name: Consistency choices
concepts.body: Replicas may return older state until changes propagate. Stronger coordination can provide stricter ordering but may reject or delay requests during partitions. The CAP trade-off concerns consistency and availability under a network partition, not a permanent instruction to choose any two labels.

concepts.name: Ordering and clocks
concepts.body: Wall clocks can differ and jump, so timestamps alone do not establish causality. Sequence numbers, versions and logical ordering help detect stale writes. Ordering within one stream or partition does not automatically imply a total order across the whole system.

e2e: A client sends a command with a stable operation identifier and deadline.
The service validates the command and durably records its effect and deduplication result.
A lost response causes a bounded retry using the same identifier, not a new operation.
The service returns the stored result; replicas converge according to the documented consistency contract.

tasks.name: Trace an ambiguous timeout
tasks.goal: Separate response failure from business failure.
steps: Draw a fictional order command that commits at second two but whose response is lost. At second three the client times out. List both plausible outcomes from the client's perspective and explain why blindly creating a new order is unsafe.

tasks.name: Work a deduplication ledger
steps: Start with balance 100 and no request IDs. Apply debit 10 with ID demo-7, store balance 90 and its result together. Repeat demo-7 twice: expected balance remains 90. A genuinely new demo-8 debit changes the balance to 80.

tasks.name: Choose partition behavior
steps: For a fictional inventory of one ticket, split two replicas. Compare accepting sales independently with requiring an authoritative quorum. The first can oversell; the second may refuse a sale despite local health. State which outcome the business prefers and why.

tasks.name: Bound retries
steps: Plan three total attempts within a two-second deadline, allowing connection time and randomized backoff. Stop retrying invalid requests. Explain why three nested services each making three attempts can create up to 27 downstream attempts for one original request.

key_terms: Partition: communication failure between system members.
Idempotency: repeated execution preserves the intended effect.
Quorum: required agreement among selected replicas.
Causality: one event influencing another.
lesson.safety: Use fictional ledgers only; do not send duplicate payment requests or disrupt real networks.
cleanup: Retain the operation trace and remove any real identifiers from diagrams before sharing.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical checkout times out after the server commits an order. How can the client safely recover?
interview_points: Treat completion as unknown rather than certainly failed.
Retry with the same durable idempotency identifier.
Store deduplication and the business effect atomically where possible.
Bound attempts and reconcile ambiguous results.

foundations/distributed-systems-fundamen.core: Timeouts do not prove non-execution. Use deadlines, bounded retries and durable idempotency. Specify partition behavior, replica freshness and ordering explicitly; do not use wall-clock timestamps as proof of causality.
prerequisites: Understand requests, responses and database writes.

storyboard.title: An order commits but its response is lost
storyboard.objective: Show why retries need a stable operation identifier.

scenes.title: Commit the order
scenes.caption: The business effect and request result become durable.
scenes.narration: The service commits order demo-7 and its deduplication result. The order exists before the client receives confirmation.

scenes.title: Response disappears
scenes.caption: The client's timeout does not undo the committed order.
scenes.narration: The response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the server failed before or after committing the order.

scenes.title: Retry without duplicating
scenes.caption: The same identifier retrieves the existing result.
scenes.narration: The client retries demo-7 within its deadline. The service reads the saved result and returns it without creating another order.

lesson.title: Capacity planning and performance baselines
lesson.why: A capacity plan translates demand into resources before queues become incidents. A baseline makes comparisons meaningful: a faster response during lighter traffic is not evidence that a configuration change improved the system.
lesson.what: Planning combines representative measurements, demand forecasts and failure headroom. Track throughput, latency distributions, errors and saturation together; averages alone hide the slow requests and burst behavior users actually experience.

concepts.name: Workload definition
concepts.body: Record arrival rate, concurrency, request mix, payload size and cache state. A read-heavy synthetic workload may miss an expensive write path. Keep the same workload definition when comparing changes, and distinguish closed-loop clients from independently arriving production traffic.

concepts.name: Latency distributions
concepts.body: Median latency describes the middle request, while p95 means 95 percent of observations are at or below that value. Tail latency grows rapidly near saturation. Do not average percentile values from different populations and call the result a global percentile.

concepts.name: Concurrency and utilization
concepts.body: For a stable system, Little's law relates average in-flight work to throughput multiplied by average time. At 100 requests per second and 0.2 seconds, average concurrency is 20. This describes steady behavior; bursts and queues require additional margin.

concepts.name: Headroom and constraints
concepts.body: Forecast demand and reserve capacity for failures, bursts and rollout overlap. Quotas, connection pools and downstream limits may bind before CPU. Scaling has a delay, so the plan must cover demand while new capacity starts rather than assuming instant unlimited supply.

e2e: Define a representative request mix and collect a reproducible baseline with timestamps.
Increase demand gradually in an isolated model and identify the first saturated resource.
Estimate forecast load plus failure and startup headroom using measured service capacity.
Set warning thresholds and compare later samples against the same workload and conditions.

tasks.name: Construct a baseline record
steps: On paper, record 100 requests per second, 80 percent reads, 20 percent writes, 10 KiB payloads and warm cache. Add p50, p95, errors and queue depth fields. Mark values as hypothetical rather than claiming a benchmark was executed.

tasks.name: Calculate in-flight work
steps: At 150 requests per second and average response time 0.4 seconds, compute 150 × 0.4 = 60 in-flight requests. If latency rises to one second at unchanged completed throughput, concurrency becomes 150; explain the resulting pressure on connection pools.

tasks.name: Plan one-instance failure
tasks.goal: Translate headroom into a fleet size.
steps: Forecast 900 requests per second and assume a measured safe rate of 300 per instance. Three instances cover normal demand but no failure. Four retain 900 after one fails; add further margin if burst or deployment requirements demand it.

tasks.name: Interpret conflicting metrics
steps: A fictional sample shows CPU at 30 percent, all 50 database connections occupied and increasing p95 latency. Propose measuring query time and queue waits before increasing application replicas, because more clients may intensify the database bottleneck.

key_terms: Baseline: documented reference measurement conditions.
p95: latency threshold covering 95 percent of observations.
Saturation: resource demand approaching available capacity.
Headroom: capacity reserved beyond expected normal demand.
lesson.safety: Use offline samples, not traffic generators against shared services. Never label synthetic numbers as measured production results.
cleanup: Keep the assumptions with each calculation and remove any unsupported benchmark claims.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical API has low CPU but high tail latency during peaks. How would you build a capacity plan?
interview_points: Define the request mix and collect comparable latency distributions.
Inspect connection, queue and downstream saturation.
Use measured safe throughput and failure headroom.
Include scaling startup time and explicit forecast assumptions.

foundations/capacity-planning-and-perfor.core: Baseline workload conditions and throughput, latency, errors and saturation together. Average concurrency equals throughput times average latency in a stable system. Size for failures and scale-up delay, not just normal average demand.
objectives: Calculate average concurrency and failure headroom.
Identify a bottleneck hidden by low CPU utilization.
prerequisites: Understand request rates and latency units.

storyboard.title: A full database pool creates an API queue
storyboard.objective: Connect demand, pool saturation and tail latency.

scenes.title: Stable baseline
scenes.caption: Requests finish while connection demand fits capacity.
scenes.narration: The baseline records request mix and latency. Workers acquire connections without a growing queue, so throughput remains stable.

scenes.title: Pool saturation
scenes.caption: CPU remains low while requests wait for connections.
scenes.narration: Longer queries occupy every connection. New requests wait, increasing in-flight work and tail latency despite idle processor capacity.

scenes.title: Plan from the bottleneck
scenes.caption: Measure query waits before adding application workers.
scenes.narration: The operator separates query execution from queue time, tests the constrained path and revises safe capacity with failure headroom.

lesson.title: Cloud account organization and landing zones
lesson.why: Unstructured cloud growth makes ownership, access and incident containment difficult. Separating workloads into governed boundaries reduces accidental cross-environment changes and makes central controls available before teams deploy their first application.
lesson.what: A landing zone is a prepared environment with identity, organizational structure, network foundations, logging and guardrails. Accounts, subscriptions and projects differ by provider, but each can form a useful administration and policy boundary.

concepts.name: Boundary design
concepts.body: Separate production, development and shared security functions according to risk and ownership. An account boundary can constrain permissions, quotas and billing visibility, but shared identities or network paths still connect environments. More accounts also create lifecycle and support work.

concepts.name: Federated access
concepts.body: Central identity federation provides short-lived access without distributing permanent administrator keys. Map groups to narrowly scoped roles and protect emergency access separately. A central identity outage needs a documented recovery path, not an undocumented shared root credential.

concepts.name: Preventive guardrails
concepts.body: Organizational policies can restrict actions available to member environments. They usually limit permissions rather than granting them. A permitted organizational action still requires an identity grant; conversely, an explicit higher-level restriction can block a seemingly correct local role.

concepts.name: Evidence and lifecycle
concepts.body: Central logs, ownership metadata and budgets make activity attributable and discoverable. Account creation should establish these controls before workload access. Retirement needs data retention decisions and dependency checks; deleting an environment is not a substitute for preserving required evidence.

e2e: Classify workloads and assign accountable owners before choosing organizational boundaries.
Create a paper hierarchy with separate production, development and security environments.
Attach baseline identity, logging and policy requirements before permitting workload deployment.
Review effective access and retirement evidence periodically as ownership and workloads change.

tasks.name: Design a small hierarchy
steps: For a fictional retailer, draw production, development and security-log accounts beneath organizational groups. Place a shared identity service explicitly. Explain why production and development should not share an unrestricted deployment role even if their billing owner is identical.

tasks.name: Evaluate permission intersection
steps: Let a role allow actions {read, write} and an organizational guardrail permit {read, list}. The effective candidate set is their intersection, {read}, assuming no other restrictions. The guardrail does not independently grant list. Record this expected result offline.

tasks.name: Specify a vending checklist
tasks.goal: Make new environments ready before use.
steps: Write required fields for owner, purpose, environment, log destination and approved access group. Reject a hypothetical request missing its owner. Include budget notifications as visibility controls, not an assertion that notifications automatically stop spending.

tasks.name: Rehearse safe retirement
steps: A project is abandoned but stores logs referenced by incident investigations. Identify retention obligations, shared network dependencies and role trusts before proposing retirement. Keep the exercise on paper; do not disable accounts or move actual organizational units.

key_terms: Landing zone: governed starting environment.
Guardrail: preventive or detective governance control.
Federation: trusting an external identity provider.
Account vending: standardized environment creation workflow.
lesson.safety: Use fictitious organizations and permission sets. Do not access root identities, change organization policies or create billable environments.
cleanup: Retain the anonymized hierarchy and checklist; remove any real account numbers if added during discussion.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical team has an administrator role but cannot perform an action in a member account. How would you investigate?
interview_points: Evaluate organizational restrictions as well as identity grants.
Check the actual account, role session and resource policy.
Remember that guardrails limit rather than grant access.
Preserve central evidence and avoid bypassing governance with root access.

foundations/cloud-account-organization-a.core: Landing zones establish boundaries, federated identity, logging and governance before workloads arrive. Organizational restrictions do not grant permissions. Treat environment creation, ownership review and retirement as controlled lifecycle operations.
objectives: Explain how a guardrail constrains an identity grant.
prerequisites: Understand identities, permissions and deployment environments.

storyboard.title: A local grant meets an organizational limit
storyboard.objective: Explain effective access across a governed account boundary.

scenes.title: Governed access
scenes.caption: Identity grants operate inside organizational limits.
scenes.narration: The deployment role requests an action. The account evaluates both its identity permissions and applicable organizational restrictions.

scenes.title: Unexpected denial
scenes.caption: A broad local role cannot override a guardrail.
scenes.narration: The organizational policy excludes writing. The request fails even though the local role includes write permission.

scenes.title: Review the intended boundary
scenes.caption: Diagnose effective access rather than bypassing governance.
scenes.narration: The owner checks the target account and policy hierarchy, then requests a reviewed exception only if the business need justifies it.
